p: General Hancock arrived by order of Meade to take command and restore order. His presence steadied the shaken troops. "I think this the strongest position by nature upon which to fight a battle that I ever saw," he reported to Meade.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (map walkthrough)
p.short: Site walkthrough stop 4, “Seminary Ridge” (The Union Retreat), paragraph 3 of 3

p: On the afternoon of July 2, Confederate forces under Hood's division discovered that Little Round Top — the rocky height anchoring the left of the Union line — was unoccupied. Law's Alabama brigade raced for the summit.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (map walkthrough)
p.short: Site walkthrough stop 5, “Little Round Top” (The Race for the Summit), paragraph 1 of 3

p: At almost the same moment, Meade's chief engineer spotted the danger and rushed Vincent's V Corps brigade to the hill. They arrived with minutes to spare.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (map walkthrough)
p.short: Site walkthrough stop 5, “Little Round Top” (The Race for the Summit), paragraph 2 of 3

p: The 20th Maine under Colonel Joshua Lawrence Chamberlain held the extreme left of the entire Union army. When the regiment's ammunition ran low after multiple Confederate assaults, Chamberlain ordered a bayonet charge downhill. The unexpected assault routed the exhausted 15th Alabama and secured the position.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (map walkthrough)
p.short: Site walkthrough stop 5, “Little Round Top” (The Race for the Summit), paragraph 3 of 3

p: Below Little Round Top, the massive boulders of Devil's Den provided a natural fortress. Hood's Texas Brigade fought its way through the rocky terrain, driving Ward's Union brigade from the position.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (map walkthrough)
p.short: Site walkthrough stop 6, “Devil's Den” (The Triangular Field), paragraph 1 of 3

p: Confederate sharpshooters occupied the crevices among the boulders and fired on Little Round Top throughout the afternoon. The famous photograph of a Confederate sharpshooter dead among the rocks was later revealed to have been staged by photographer Alexander Gardner.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (map walkthrough)
p.short: Site walkthrough stop 6, “Devil's Den” (The Triangular Field), paragraph 2 of 3

p: The fighting in the triangular field between Devil's Den and the Wheatfield was some of the most confused and brutal of the entire battle.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (map walkthrough)
p.short: Site walkthrough stop 6, “Devil's Den” (The Triangular Field), paragraph 3 of 3

p: The 26-acre Wheatfield of farmer George Rose became one of the bloodiest patches of ground in American military history on the afternoon of July 2. The field changed hands at least six times during three hours of fighting.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (map walkthrough)
p.short: Site walkthrough stop 7, “The Wheatfield” (Six Times Contested), paragraph 1 of 3

p: Kershaw's South Carolina brigade attacked through Rose's Woods. de Trobriand's brigade and then Sweitzer's formed successive defensive lines. Caldwell's entire II Corps division — all four brigades under Cross, Kelly, Zook, and Brooke — countercharged through the field.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (map walkthrough)
p.short: Site walkthrough stop 7, “The Wheatfield” (Six Times Contested), paragraph 2 of 3

p: Brigadier General Samuel Zook was mortally wounded leading his brigade into the fight. Colonel Patrick Kelly's Irish Brigade advanced with green sprigs of boxwood in their caps, a Celtic tradition before battle. By nightfall, approximately 4,000 men lay killed or wounded in this single field.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (map walkthrough)
p.short: Site walkthrough stop 7, “The Wheatfield” (Six Times Contested), paragraph 3 of 3

p: General Daniel Sickles, the controversial III Corps commander, advanced his corps a mile forward from the assigned position on Cemetery Ridge to the higher ground around the Peach Orchard. The move created a vulnerable salient with exposed flanks on both sides.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (map walkthrough)
p.short: Site walkthrough stop 8, “Peach Orchard” (Sickles' Salient Falls), paragraph 1 of 3

p: Barksdale's Mississippi brigade — 1,400 men — charged the Peach Orchard with Barksdale riding at their front. The assault swept through the orchard and shattered the III Corps.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (map walkthrough)
p.short: Site walkthrough stop 8, “Peach Orchard” (Sickles' Salient Falls), paragraph 2 of 3

p: Sickles himself was struck by a cannonball that mangled his leg. He was carried from the field smoking a cigar, reportedly to reassure his men. His leg was amputated; he later donated it to the Army Medical Museum, where he visited it annually for the rest of his life.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (map walkthrough)
p.short: Site walkthrough stop 8, “Peach Orchard” (Sickles' Salient Falls), paragraph 3 of 3

p: As darkness fell on July 2, Hays' Louisiana Tigers and Avery's North Carolina brigade launched a twilight assault on Cemetery Hill. The attackers swept up the slope and overran Wiedrich's and Ricketts' batteries.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (map walkthrough)
p.short: Site walkthrough stop 9, “Cemetery Hill” (The Tigers Assault the Guns), paragraph 1 of 3

p: For ten desperate minutes, Confederate soldiers fought among the Union cannon with rammers, handspikes, and bare hands. It was the closest any Confederate force came to capturing Cemetery Hill during the entire battle.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (map walkthrough)
p.short: Site walkthrough stop 9, “Cemetery Hill” (The Tigers Assault the Guns), paragraph 2 of 3

p: Brigadier General Isaac Avery was mortally wounded during the advance. As he lay dying, he scrawled a final message on a scrap of paper using his own blood: "Tell my father I died with my face to the enemy." Carroll's II Corps brigade countercharged and drove the Confederates back down the hill.
